The paper you are referring to is titled "Reciprocal classes of random walks on graphs", authored by mathematicians Giovanni Conforti and Christian Léonard. It was published on arXiv in May 2015 and later appeared in the journal Stochastic Processes and their Applications (2017). 
arXiv.org
 +1
📌 Core Concept & Definitions
Reciprocal Class: The reciprocal class of a reference Markov path measure is defined as the set of all mixtures of its bridges. In simpler terms, if two processes share exactly the same bridge measures (the probability distribution of paths conditioned on starting at a specific point 
𝑥
𝑥
 and ending at a specific point 
𝑦
𝑦
 over a given time interval), they belong to the same reciprocal class.
Setting: The authors analyze this within the framework of a continuous-time Markov random walk on a graph. 
arXiv
 +2
🔑 Key Methodologies & Characterizations
The paper provides two primary ways to mathematically characterize the reciprocal class: 
www.semanticscholar.org
Reciprocal Characteristics: The main result introduces specific invariants called reciprocal characteristics. The crucial property of these characteristics is that their algebraic expression depends only on the jump intensity of the random walk. This allows researchers to explicitly check if another process belongs to the same class without knowing the full distribution. 
arXiv.org
 +1
Short-Time Taylor Expansions: As a second approach, the authors characterize the reciprocal class through Taylor expansions in small time of certain conditional probabilities. Looking at the asymptotic behavior of the bridges over tiny time intervals yields local invariants that define the class. 
arXiv.org
 +1
💡 Why It Matters
Prior to this work, finding reciprocal invariants for jump processes with discrete state spaces was mostly limited to simple counting processes or strict geometric conditions. Conforti and Léonard used a rigorous measure-theoretical approach that significantly extended these boundaries, linking reciprocal processes directly to the graph-theoretic structure of the underlying random walk. This framework connects deeply with the discrete Schrödinger problem and optimal transport on graphs.
